transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, I suppose what brings me in is… I just feel like I’m always on the go, even when there’s no reason to be. Like I’ll start with the garden club list, then suddenly I’m digging through my knitting bag, and then I remember I need to look at travel papers—oh, and those papers are still on the dining table from last week—and I haven’t really finished any one thing. It’s like I’m up and moving from one thing to the next all day, even on a quiet day.
When you’re like this, do you need much less sleep than usual?

I don’t know that I’d say I need much less sleep, no. I mean, I might get myself all stirred up doing little things around the house, and then I’m thinking about the next day, or whether I watered the plants—my neighbor gave me this fern that’s very fussy—but… as far as sleep being way less than usual, I haven’t really noticed that.
When you find yourself constantly moving from one task to another, is it because your mind is filled with worry?

I’m not sure it’s worry, exactly. I mean, sometimes I’ll think, “Oh, I should get that done,” and then that reminds me of something else, and off I go. Like the other day I went to put away a teacup and ended up sorting coupons in a drawer—I don’t even use half of them. But I wouldn’t say my head is full of worry the whole time. It’s more like one thing just pulls me to the next.
Thinking back to when you were a child, were you already the kind of person who had trouble staying focused on one task?

Oh yes, I think so. Back in grade school, my teachers used to tell my mother I was bright, but… scattered, that was the word they used. I’d lose papers, talk when I wasn’t supposed to, and I remember being told to sit still because I’d be wiggling around before I even finished my work. My mother kept a little folder of notes from teachers—though where that ended up, I have no idea. She saved everything, buttons, report cards, old church programs… but yes, I was like that even then.
Do you still often feel physically restless, like it’s hard to stay seated when you need to?

Yes, I do get that, especially if I’m supposed to sit for a long stretch. I start feeling sort of stirred up inside, like I ought to get up and straighten a cushion or go see if I left something in the kitchen. It’s not always dramatic, but it’s hard to just stay put.
Do you often blurt things out or interrupt people before they’ve finished speaking?

Yes, I do, more than I like to admit. My husband tells me I cut him off before he’s finished his sentence, and I’ll say, “I know, I know,” even when maybe I don’t know exactly where he was going with it. And in group planning things—like at church or with the ladies’ luncheon—I’ll jump in because I’m afraid if I don’t say it right then, the thought will just fly out of my head. Then afterward I think, oh dear, I probably talked over someone again.
Do you still often have trouble focusing on what someone is saying, even when you’re trying to listen?

Yes, that does happen. I’ll start out really trying to listen, like at a planning meeting at church, and I’m nodding along, but then a few minutes later I realize I’ve missed half of what was said. Same with reading the church bulletin—I’ll read down the page and then think, wait, what did that say about Tuesday? So yes, even when I mean to pay attention, it sort of slips away from me.
Do other people often describe you as fidgety or unable to stay still?

Yes, people do say that sometimes. My husband will notice it more than anyone—if we’re watching television, I’ll be tapping my foot or rubbing my fingers together, or fussing with the blanket in my lap. I don’t always realize I’m doing it until someone points it out. Same thing in meetings, I’ll be sitting there trying to be still, and then I catch myself fiddling with my purse strap or whatever’s in my hands.
Have you often gotten into serious trouble for breaking rules or getting into fights?

No, I don’t think so. I mean, I’ve had times where I got scolded or someone was upset with me, but serious trouble for breaking rules or fights—no, not really. I was never the fighting type. I’d be more likely to get flustered and talk too much, and then later think, why did I say all that? But no, nothing like serious trouble that I can think of.

final_diagnosis.reason: The interview supports attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder with persistent symptoms from childhood into adulthood. The patient confirms longstanding inattention (losing focus while listening/reading, being scattered, losing papers, not finishing tasks), hyperactivity/restlessness (always on the go, difficulty staying seated, fidgeting), and impulsivity (interrupting/blurting out). Childhood onset is clearly established by teacher reports and maternal recollection. Mania is less likely because decreased need for sleep is denied, and anxiety-driven restlessness is not supported because the patient does not describe pervasive worry as the cause.
